transgress

trans-GRESS · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To transgress is to misbehave or break the rules, especially a moral or legal boundary.

The knight feared he had transgressed some unspoken code of honor by accepting the bribe.

Example

Employees who transgress the company's confidentiality policy face immediate dismissal.

This wasn't a minor slip-up -- it was crossing a clearly defined boundary the rules had drawn, which is exactly transgress.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

violate: Violate means to break a specific, stated rule, agreement, or right -- a contract, a treaty, a speed limit. Transgress is wider and more moral in flavor: you can transgress an unspoken social code or a boundary no document ever wrote down.

infringe: Infringe means to edge over a line in a way that limits someone else's rights or territory -- patents, copyrights, personal freedoms. Transgress does not need a victim: it is the act of crossing a clearly understood boundary, whether or not anyone is harmed.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

comply: act in accordance with a rule or request

Where it sits · how far over the line one goes

bend → transgress → sin

bend vs. transgress: Bending a rule stretches it without quite breaking it; transgressing it crosses the line outright.

sin vs. transgress: To transgress is to cross any line that was clearly drawn; sin goes further up this scale, breaking a religious or spiritual law -- the gravest kind of line there is.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — trans-: across, beyond (Latin)

root — gress: to step, walk (Latin (gradi))

Put it together: Transgress comes from Latin trans- ('across, beyond') + gradi ('to step, walk') -- literally 'to step across' a boundary.

Use the root in a new word: progress: The same gradi root gives us progress (pro- 'forward' + gradi, 'to step forward').

Root Check

Word Choice

Transgress can describe breaking a written law, an unspoken social code, or a moral or religious boundary -- the common thread is crossing a line that was clearly understood to exist.
